short.headline: Dementia already affects 88 lakh Indians over 60
short.dek: And the true cost is hidden: two-thirds of it is unpaid family care, mostly by women, while even the medical bills come out of household pockets.
short.body: About one in thirteen Indians over 60 lives with dementia, an estimated 88 lakh people, according to India's first nationally representative clinical study, LASI-DAD. That number is projected to nearly double to 1.69 crore by 2036 as the country ages. But the financial toll starts long before diagnosis: US evidence shows household wealth begins to erode years earlier due to impaired judgement. In India, where most dementia goes undiagnosed and care falls on families, the cost is largely invisible, paid in lost wages, drained savings, and the time of daughters and daughters-in-law.

macha.heading: Okay, but what does this actually mean, macha?
macha.body: Dementia is not just forgetting names. It slowly takes away a person's ability to handle money, to plan, to judge. The sickness itself is heavy, but the money side is sneaky. This data shows that for every 100 Indians over 60, about 7 to 8 have dementia — that's over 88 lakh people, and it will almost double in 20 years. The real cost in India is not hospital bills; it's the daughter who leaves her job to care for a parent, the gold sold to pay for medicines, the family that doesn't know the confusion is a disease and not just old age.
macha.soWhat: Dementia's price tag is mostly invisible, and it's paid by the women of the household.

article.title: What dementia costs India
article.standfirst: Dementia already burdens 88 lakh older Indians, and the toll is set to nearly double by 2036. The real cost is not in hospitals, it is hidden in unpaid care, lost earnings, and household savings spent on a disease that often goes unnamed.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## How quickly does dementia rise with age?

Dementia barely registers when you turn sixty. LASI-DAD, India's first nationally representative clinical dementia study, estimated that only 2.9% of people aged 60 to 64 have it. But after that, the numbers begin to climb sharply. By 70, about one in ten (10.3%) of the 70 to 74 age group live with the condition. By 85, it is a quarter (25.4%). The rise roughly doubles every five years after 70, so each extra decade brings a step-change in risk. This is why the absolute number of dementia cases will keep swelling: India is ageing, and age is the single strongest driver of the disease.

## How many people does that actually mean?

Using the 2016 population, the study put the national headcount at 88 lakh Indians over 60 with dementia. Because the proportion of older people is growing, even if the risk at every age stays the same, the number of people living with dementia is projected to hit 1.69 crore by 2036. That is a near-doubling in just twenty years. These are not forecasts of suddenly worse disease; they are demographic arithmetic. When more people survive past 70, more people will develop dementia. The health system and families will have to care for almost twice as many patients.

## Who carries more: women, and rural India

Dementia does not fall equally. Among Indians 60 and older, an estimated 9.0% of women have dementia, against 5.8% of men. The rural prevalence is 8.4%, against 5.3% in cities. The female gap partly reflects a simple truth: women live longer, and more of them reach the highest-risk ages. But there is more to it than survival. These are crude numbers, not adjusted for education or other factors, so they are associations, not clean causes. Yet the pattern matters. The people most likely to have dementia are also the people least likely to get a diagnosis and most likely to depend on unpaid care from other women.

## Does education make a difference?

The steepest gradient of all is schooling. LASI-DAD found that among older adults with no formal schooling, prevalence was 10.3%. For those who had up to primary schooling, it dropped to 4.5%. And for those with middle school or higher education, it fell to just 1.5%. This does not mean books are a vaccine. Education captures a lifetime of better nutrition, higher income, and more health-seeking behaviour. There may also be a real biological effect: more-schooled brains might cope longer before symptoms appear, a concept called cognitive reserve. But detection could also be harder in less-educated groups, so the true gap might be narrower. At any rate, the least privileged Indians face the highest measured burden.

## Which states are hit hardest?

The map of dementia across India runs from about 4.5% of older adults in Delhi to roughly 11% in Jammu & Kashmir. Generally, states in the south and east show higher prevalence, while the north-western plains show lower. The north-eastern states, except Assam, were published only as a single group at 7.35%. Several small states and union territories have no estimate at all, so the map is incomplete. These state numbers are modelled from a sample, not census-level counts. They are a start, but they leave large gaps, especially in the hill states and the heartland.

## Have deaths from dementia really risen eightfold?

Recorded deaths from Alzheimer's and other dementias have climbed from about 17,000 in 1980 to over 1.4 lakh in 2023, according to IHME's Global Burden of Disease modelled estimates. The rise is not because dementia is new. More Indians are living into old age, and fewer are dying young from infections, so dementia emerges on death certificates. But there is a catch. Dementia is widely under-recorded as a cause of death, so even this eightfold rise is a floor. The sharp jump after 2021 partly reflects a change in how deaths were coded, not a sudden crisis. Focus on the forty-year climb rather than the last kink.

## What does America tell us about money slipping away before a diagnosis?

A careful US study, following households over decades, found that money trouble starts years before anyone says the word 'dementia'. Compared with similar dementia-free households, those heading toward dementia began to fall behind in net worth about six years before diagnosis. At diagnosis, the gap was roughly US$51,000. Four years later, it had widened to roughly US$125,000. The researchers ruled out overspending or heavy medical bills. Earnings dipped only slightly right at onset. Placebo conditions like cancer and heart disease showed no such wealth gap. The mechanism was not a spending spree but a slow erosion of judgement. Money was slipping away through poor decisions, not high expenses.

## Where exactly does the wealth leak from?

The American data shows the gap sitting in the assets that demand active management. Two years before dementia was diagnosed, households who would develop dementia held about US$89,400 in stocks, bonds, and mutual funds. Their dementia-free peers held US$112,600. In checking and savings accounts, the gap was smaller. Retirement accounts were lower but not dramatically so. The losses were concentrated in market-linked securities, the kind of assets that require monitoring, rebalancing, and decision-making. The study concluded that impaired financial capacity, not excess spending, was the driver. In India, very few elderly hold stock portfolios, but land, gold, and small businesses are similar in one way: they need sound judgement to manage, and that judgement erodes silently.

## What is the real cost of dementia care?

A global report from Alzheimer's Disease International gave a snapshot for 2010. In low-income countries, the societal cost per person with dementia was just US$868 a year. In lower-middle income, India's band, it was US$3,109. In upper-middle income, US$6,827. And in high-income countries, US$32,865. The numbers look like a steep income tax, but they describe different kinds of cost. In rich countries, most of that US$32,865 is paid services and care homes. In India's band, most of the US$3,109 is not an invoice at all. It is the time of family members. The disease is not ten times cheaper here; it is ten times less formally paid for.

There is one way to attach a rupee figure to the private medical hit, though it has to be read carefully. In the same US study, families heading into dementia were paying only modestly more out of pocket on health than similar families, about US$1,600 a year more, not nearly enough to explain the wealth gap but a real cost all the same. Converted into Indian purchasing power, that is very roughly 35,000 to 40,000 rupees a year. Treat it as an illustration, not a measurement: it is American data, a purchasing-power conversion is not an actual Indian price, and the two health systems are worlds apart. What survives the translation is the size and the direction, a few tens of thousands of rupees a year in direct medical costs, sitting on top of unpaid care that is worth far more and is counted nowhere.

## Why does the cost look so low in India?

Because two-thirds of it never shows up in a budget. In lower-middle income countries, 65% of the total cost of dementia was informal, unpaid family care. In low-income countries, it was 58%. In high-income countries, it was 40%. Unpaid does not mean free. It is paid in the loss of a daughter's or daughter-in-law's wages, in years of work forgone, in the exhaustion that no insurance policy covers. Because this labour is not bought and sold, it is invisible in national accounts. India, with limited care homes and almost no dementia-specific insurance, leans almost entirely on this invisible workforce.

## Why does it land so heavily on families?

Even the medical slice of dementia care comes straight out of household pockets. India's National Health Accounts show that the share of total health spending paid directly by families was 64.2% in 2014. By 2023, it had fallen to 43.4%. That is real progress, but it still means that when a person with dementia needs a doctor's visit, a brain scan, or a month of medicines, the bill lands on the family. Dementia is a long, slowly worsening condition, so these bills pile up over years. Combine that with the unpaid nursing, and you see why a dementia diagnosis can drain savings, sell gold, and push a family into debt.

## Is this only about dementia, or about all of us getting old?

You do not need a diagnosis to start handling money worse. Researchers who studied millions of real financial choices in the United States found that the sharpest age for managing money is somewhere around the early fifties, and that the skill slips quietly from there, well inside the range of ordinary ageing. Dementia is the sharp end of that slope, not a separate country. The American study at the heart of this piece showed the financial damage beginning about six years before anyone had a name for the illness, and it was not lost wages, not hospital bills, not a late-life spending spree. It was judgement going on the decisions that need active attention. The difference is what waits at the bottom of the slope. In America there were pensions and a public safety net. In India there is far less. By the official ageing survey, only about one in five retired Indians draws any pension at all, and nearly four in five neither receive nor expect one. Most older Indians manage land, gold, a small shop and a bank account on their own, with no annuity and no long-term-care insurance to catch a bad call. The slope is the same. The cushion is thinner.

## In India, the slipping money has a name: the scam

When judgement goes, the money does not vanish. It moves to someone, a fraudster, a sharp counterparty, a relative who senses an opening. American research found that the people who score worst at spotting a scam are measurably more likely to develop dementia in the years that follow, so falling for a con can be an early symptom rather than simple bad luck. Other studies caught the first signs in missed bills and slipping credit long before any clinic was involved. Now set that against the India an older person actually lives in. In 2024 alone, Indians lost close to 2,000 crore rupees to a single kind of fraud, the "digital arrest" scam, where callers posing as police freeze a victim with fear and drain their accounts, across more than a lakh complaints to the national cybercrime portal. That loss has multiplied several times over in just a couple of years. Here is the honest catch, and it is the whole point of this piece. Nobody can tell you how many of those victims were old, because India does not count it. The home ministry has told Parliament that cybercrime against the elderly is not recorded separately. What the crime statistics do show, narrowly, is around 3,200 cases of forgery, cheating and fraud against people over sixty in a single year, and even that counts only what reached a police station. A confused parent who signs a paper, wires money to a stranger, or hands savings to a smooth relative almost never files a complaint. The loss is real and the record is mostly blank.

## Why does no one catch it in time?

Because the person losing the money usually cannot see it, and in India almost no one around them is looking either. Studies of older adults keep finding that people are the last to notice their own decline, which is exactly why they go on signing, lending and deciding long after they should have handed the pen to someone else. India makes this far worse. By the best available estimate, only about one in ten Indians with dementia is ever diagnosed. The other nine are simply old people who have grown forgetful and hard to manage. For generations the confusion has been read as a normal part of getting old rather than an illness, something a family absorbs at home instead of taking to a doctor. So the signal a more aware household might act on, the strange decision, the money gone missing, the same mistake again, gets waved away as old age until the savings are already spent. And the people least likely to get that diagnosis are, as the earlier numbers showed, the ones with the least schooling and the least to spare in the first place.

## So what actually protects a family?

The most useful finding in the American study is also the most hopeful one. Among families who got a timely diagnosis, the financial bleeding slowed and sometimes reversed, because once everyone knew, someone else took over the money. Among those diagnosed late or never, it kept going. The lesson is not really about doctors. It is about handing over financial control early, while the person can still choose to do it. In an Indian joint family that ought to be a strength, since there is usually a son, a daughter or a spouse close enough to notice. The trouble, which researchers have seen too, is that the handover tends to come too slowly, long after the first bad decisions. The protections that work are unglamorous and available today. Add nominees and a second name to bank accounts. Set up a power of attorney early, not in the middle of a crisis. Move the savings that need constant watching into things that need less of it, a fixed deposit or a pension annuity rather than a portfolio someone has to manage. Use the banking help the regulator already requires for senior citizens. And know that the law has quietly seen this coming. Under the 2007 senior citizens law, property an elderly parent signs over to a child who then fails to care for them is "deemed to have been made by fraud or coercion or under undue influence", and a tribunal can void it. The state already assumes that some of what the old sign away, they were in no fit state to sign. The kindest thing a family can do is make sure it never reaches that point.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Longitudinal Aging Study in India – Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia. A nationally representative survey that sent trained clinicians to assess cognitive function in a sample of older Indians, instead of using hospital records.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It provides India's first robust, home-grown estimate of how common dementia really is — the backbone of every figure on this page.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The share of people in a group who have a condition at a given time. Think 'how many in every hundred have it right now', not 'how many will ever get it'.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: All the percentages shown (2.9%, 9%, etc.) are prevalence — the burden sitting in the community today.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A range around an estimate that reflects statistical uncertainty. If the study were repeated 100 times, the true value would fall inside this range 95 times. It does not mean there is a 95% chance the true value is inside — that is a common misinterpretation.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: LASI-DAD's estimate of 7.4% (95% CI 6.35–8.51) reminds us that the number is not exact; the real prevalence is likely somewhere in that band.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A summary rate that imagines each country had the same age distribution (a standard population). It strips out the effect of a country's age mix so we can compare disease risk fairly.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India's crude prevalence looks low because India is young. Age-standardised rates show the risk is not so different from richer, older countries.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A huge, continuously updated study by IHME that models health loss from hundreds of diseases for every country, combining surveys, hospital data, and death records to fill gaps.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: GBD provides the only long-run trend of dementia deaths for India; without it, we would have almost no mortality numbers.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A conversion rate that compares what money actually buys in different countries, instead of using market exchange rates. US$1 converted at PPP buys a basket of goods in India similar to what US$1 buys in the US.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It is the least misleading way to turn a US medical-cost number into a rough rupee illustration, but it remains an illustration, not an actual Indian price.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The share of all health spending in a country that is paid directly by households at the point of care — not through insurance, government schemes, or employers.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: High OOPE means even diagnosed dementia care drains family budgets immediately, on top of the unpaid nursing.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The sum of all money spent on health in a country in a year, from government budgets, insurance, employers, and households.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: When we say OOPE is 43.4%, that is 43.4% of this total. The denominator is all health spending, not just the private market.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Unpaid care provided by family members — bathing, feeding, watching, managing money — that replaces what would be paid professional or institutional care in a richer system.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: In India, roughly two-thirds of the total cost of dementia is this invisible labour, and it shows up nowhere in budgets or insurance claims.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The brain's ability to improvise and find alternate ways of getting a job done, built up over a lifetime of education, complex work, and social engagement. It does not prevent the underlying disease, but it can delay the point at which symptoms appear.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The steep education gradient in dementia prevalence is partly explained by cognitive reserve — more-schooled brains may cope longer before clinical detection — but education also brings better nutrition and health care, so the effect is mixed.

chartExplainers.title: Dementia climbs steeply with age
chartExplainers.takeaway: Dementia leaps from 2.9% at ages 60-64 to 25.4% past 85.
chartExplainers.detail: The bars show the percentage of people in each five-year age band who live with dementia, from the LASI-DAD clinical survey. At 60 to 64, it is just 2.9%. At 65 to 69, 4.0%. Then it climbs: 10.3% at 70-74, 13.3% at 75-79, 16.3% at 80-84, and finally 25.4% for those 85 and older. The pattern is unmistakable: the risk roughly doubles every five years after 70. This is not a small statistical wobble; it is the central reason why an ageing India will see a surge in dementia cases. For a family, it means that a healthy 65-year-old has a low chance today, but a parent who lives past 80 faces a one-in-four chance.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This is the first thing to grasp: dementia is overwhelmingly a condition of late old age. Without this chart, the sheer force of age as a driver remains hidden.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar represents a different age group among adults 60 and older. Read the height of the bar as the share within that group who have dementia.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not mistake these numbers for the chance of getting dementia eventually. They are the share who have it right now in that age bracket.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars are easy to scan on a phone; keep labels short and values clear.

chartExplainers.title: 88 lakh now, 1.69 crore by 2036
chartExplainers.takeaway: The number of Indians 60+ with dementia will nearly double from 88 lakh to 1.69 crore in twenty years due to ageing alone.
chartExplainers.detail: The two bars (or points) show estimated dementia cases in 2016 (88 lakh) and a projection for 2036 (1.69 crore). The projection assumes that the risk of dementia at each age stays the same as it is today. What changes is the number of older people. India's 60+ population is growing fast. So even without any increase in the disease rate per person, the sheer volume of patients almost doubles. That means double the need for care, double the burden on families, and double the financial strain. This is not a worst-case scenario; it is the baseline.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The raw count matters because health systems and families plan for numbers of people, not percentages. This chart turns a percentage into a scale that anyone can understand.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the first data point (2016) with the second (2036). The gap between them is the effect of demographic change.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is not a trend of rising incidence per person; it is a projection of higher total cases because more people will live into old age.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A simple change card or two-bar comparison works well on a small screen; avoid multiple lines.

chartExplainers.title: Who carries more: women, and rural India
chartExplainers.takeaway: Women (9.0%) and rural residents (8.4%) have notably higher crude dementia prevalence than men (5.8%) and urban residents (5.3%).
chartExplainers.detail: These crude prevalence numbers come from LASI-DAD. They are not adjusted for age or education, so they reflect real-world differences in the population mix, not necessarily biological causes. Women live longer on average, so more of them reach the highest-risk ages. Rural India has lower average education and less access to health care, both linked to higher dementia risk. The pattern matters because the people most likely to have dementia are also the most likely to rely on unpaid family care, which falls disproportionately on women.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Dementia is not evenly spread. Seeing who carries the highest burden helps target awareness and support.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the pairs of bars. The first pair shows sex difference; the second shows residence difference. Small percentage gaps mask millions of people.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not interpret these gaps as proof that being female or living in a village causes dementia. They are associations, tangled with many other factors.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Paired horizontal bars keep the comparison clear on a phone screen.

chartExplainers.title: Dementia falls sharply with schooling
chartExplainers.takeaway: Dementia prevalence drops from 10.3% among those with no schooling to 1.5% among those with middle school or more.
chartExplainers.detail: LASI-DAD divided older Indians by education level: no formal schooling (10.3% prevalence), primary or less (4.5%), and middle school or higher (1.5%). This gap is the steepest of any risk factor measured. Education is not a direct protective shield; it is a marker for a lifetime of advantages: better nutrition, more income, and complex mental activity that may build 'cognitive reserve'. But detection may also play a role. People with more schooling might answer test questions differently, or their symptoms might be noticed later. The relationship is real and large, but the reasons are tangled.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Education's link to dementia is as dramatic as it is complex. It shows how inequality gets etched into the brain.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The three bars represent three broad education groups. Note the steep drop from the first to the third bar.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read this as 'schooling prevents dementia'. It is an association, and the evidence cannot untangle all the reasons. Also, the 1.5% is not a floor for all time; risk still rises with age even in the most-educated.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Three horizontal bars are clean and instantly readable on a phone.

chartExplainers.title: Where dementia is most common
chartExplainers.takeaway: State prevalence ranges from about 4.5% in Delhi to roughly 11% in Jammu & Kashmir, with higher rates in the south and east.
chartExplainers.detail: The choropleth map would shade each state by the estimated percentage of adults 60+ with dementia. The range spans from about 4.5% in Delhi to roughly 11% in Jammu & Kashmir. The south and east appear generally higher; the north-western plains are lower. Important caveats: several small states and union territories have no estimate (they would appear blank). The north-eastern states, except Assam, are combined into a single group at 7.35%. This map is based on a sample, not a census, so state numbers carry wider uncertainty. Gaps in the map also mean we know less about the hill states.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: A map makes the geographic variation immediate. It can prompt questions about why some places look so different.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Darker shading means higher estimated prevalence. Tapping or hovering reveals the number for that state. White areas lack data.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume that a state's rate reflects its health today. Migration, age structure, and historical education all matter. Missing states mean the picture is incomplete.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Choropleths can be tricky on phones; interactive tooltips and a clear legend help.

chartExplainers.title: Deaths recorded from dementia have risen eightfold
chartExplainers.takeaway: Modelled dementia deaths rose from about 17,000 in 1980 to over 1.4 lakh in 2023, but remain severely undercounted.
chartExplainers.detail: The line chart plots annual deaths attributed to Alzheimer's and other dementias, as modelled by the Global Burden of Disease study. It starts near 17,000 in 1980 and climbs to over 1.4 lakh by 2023. The rise reflects both real increases from an ageing population and improved coding of deaths. The steep jump after 2021 is partly a statistical artifact from a coding change, so the focus should be on the long climb. But even this eightfold rise is likely an undercount. Dementia is often omitted from death certificates, so the true death toll is higher.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Dementia is emerging as a major cause of death as other killers recede. The trend signals a growing burden.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Follow the line from left to right. The steep rise in recent years is partly a data artifact, so compare the 1980 and 2010 levels for the real trend.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are modelled estimates, not exact death counts from certificates. Do not take the year-to-year wiggles as precise; the overall climb is the message.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A line chart with sparse x-axis labels (e.g., every five years) is mobile-friendly.

chartExplainers.title: America: money trouble starts before the diagnosis
chartExplainers.takeaway: US households heading toward dementia see their net worth fall behind by roughly US$125,000 four years after diagnosis, with the gap opening six years before.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows the wealth gap, in thousands of US dollars, between people who will develop dementia and matched controls who do not. At six years before diagnosis, there is no gap. By four years before, a US$16,800 gap appears. It deepens to US$38,200 at two years, US$51,200 at diagnosis, US$69,300 two years after, and US$124,800 four years after. The researchers checked for increased spending or medical bills and found none. Other diseases like cancer showed no such pattern. The conclusion: impaired financial decision-making, not overspending, slowly drains wealth.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This is US data, but the mechanism — money slipping away before anyone realises — is a stark warning for Indian families.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar represents a point in time relative to dementia diagnosis. Negative values mean less net worth than similar dementia-free households.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The dollar amounts are US numbers and do not apply to India. Only the pattern of early, silent financial decline is relevant.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with a clear x-axis label keep the progression readable.

chartExplainers.title: America: the gap sits in hard-to-manage assets
chartExplainers.takeaway: Two years before dementia onset, future patients hold significantly less in stocks, bonds, and mutual funds than controls, while cash and retirement accounts show smaller gaps.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart compares asset holdings for cases (developing dementia) and controls (similar, no dementia) two years before onset. For stocks, bonds, and mutual funds, cases held US$89,400 vs US$112,600 for controls — a US$23,200 gap. Checking and savings accounts: US$60,000 vs US$86,000. Retirement accounts (IRAs): US$34,000 vs US$49,400. The gap is largest in the market-linked assets that need active monitoring and decisions. Since earnings barely differed, the study argues that impaired financial capacity, not reduced income, explains the wealth erosion.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It pinpoints where the money is lost — not in spending, but in assets that require sound judgement. In India, land, gold, or family loans may be similarly vulnerable.
chartExplainers.howToRead: For each asset type, compare the dark bar (cases) with the light bar (controls). The biggest gap is in the first pair.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Again, US asset classes. Do not assume elderly Indians hold these exact assets. The lesson is about the type of asset: those that need decisions.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Grouped bars work if kept to a few categories; on phones, a paired list with values can be clearer.

chartExplainers.title: What a year of dementia care costs
chartExplainers.takeaway: In India's lower-middle income band, the estimated societal cost is US$3,109 per person, a fraction of the US$32,865 in rich countries — but the figures measure different things.
chartExplainers.detail: Using 2010 data, the World Alzheimer Report shows steep cost differences by country income. Low-income: US$868. Lower-middle income (India's group): US$3,109. Upper-middle: US$6,827. High-income: US$32,865. The tenfold gap between high and lower-middle income is not about cheaper illness. It is about what is counted. In rich countries, most of the cost is paid care, residential facilities, and medical services. In India, most care is provided for free by family, so it is invisible in these numbers. The chart is a starting point, but it must be read with the next chart.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The headline numbers make dementia look cheap in India. They hide the true cost that the next chart reveals.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the four bars, but pay attention to the labels: these are societal costs, not out-of-pocket spending. The composition of that cost is even more important.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not quote the US$3,109 as a typical Indian family's spending. That figure is largely imputed time, not cash.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with a log scale or clear annotations help with the wide range.

chartExplainers.title: The poorer the country, the more care is unpaid
chartExplainers.takeaway: In India's income band, 65% of dementia cost is unpaid family care, versus 40% in high-income countries.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows the share of total dementia cost that is informal (unpaid) care. In low-income countries, it is 58%. In lower-middle income, 65%. In high-income, only 40%. The pattern is the inverse of the cost chart: where official costs are high, unpaid care is low, and vice versa. In India, roughly two-thirds of the economic burden is the time and labour of family members. That labour does not appear in GDP, health budgets, or insurance claims. But it has a huge cost: a daughter who stops working, a daughter-in-law who delays education, a family that sells land because there is no other way.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart is the key to understanding why dementia's true cost in India is invisible. It shifts the lens from money to time.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Three bars show the percentage of total cost that is informal care. Compare the middle bar (India's band) with the right bar (rich countries).
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Unpaid care is not cost-free. Do not interpret a lower dollar cost as a lower burden. The burden is shifted onto families, mostly women.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Three bars are easy; label the percentages clearly.

chartExplainers.title: Why it lands on families: India pays out of pocket
chartExplainers.takeaway: Out-of-pocket spending is still 43.4% of all health spending, so even medical dementia costs hit household budgets directly.
chartExplainers.detail: The line chart tracks the share of total health expenditure (THE) that Indian households pay directly, from 2014 to 2023. It fell from 64.2% to 43.4% over that period. That is a welcome decline, but it means that for every Rs 100 spent on health care in India, Rs 43.4 comes straight from family pockets. Dementia care often involves repeated doctor visits, medicines, and sometimes paid attendants. With most elderly Indians lacking health insurance, these costs pile up directly on families, compounding the unpaid care work.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Even the 'formal' medical costs of dementia are largely uninsured in India. This chart connects the dots between the health system's financing and the household's burden.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch the line from left to right. The trend is down, which is good, but the current level is still high.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is the share of all health care, not dementia alone. But because dementia is chronic and debilitating, out-of-pocket costs are especially punishing.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A simple line chart with a few axis labels is mobile-friendly.

sourceNotes: LASI-DAD: Lee et al., Alzheimer's & Dementia 2023, 19(7):2898-2912 (doi:10.1002/alz.12928; open access at PMC10338640). India's first nationally representative, clinically adjudicated dementia prevalence estimate, 2018-20 wave.
GBD: Global Burden of Disease Study 2023, IHME. Modelled annual deaths from Alzheimer's & other dementias, India, 1980-2023.
NBER: Li, McGarry, Nicholas & Skinner, NBER Working Paper 34659. US Health & Retirement Study data on wealth and dementia onset.
World Alzheimer Report 2010: Alzheimer's Disease International; Wimo & Prince. Societal cost per person by country income group (2010 USD).
National Health Accounts: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, India. Out-of-pocket expenditure as % of total health expenditure, 2014-2023.
caveats: All LASI-DAD figures are modelled estimates from a sample survey; they carry statistical uncertainty.
The US wealth-gap evidence is from a different country and health system; the dollar amounts do not translate, but the mechanism of pre-diagnosis financial decline may be relevant.

The mechanism linking cognitive decline to financial loss is borrowed from US research (NBER Working Paper 34659 and the wider literature on cognitive ageing and household finance). India has no comparable longitudinal study, so it is applied here as a lens, not measured.

India does not publish fraud losses by victim age; the home ministry has confirmed cybercrime against the elderly is not recorded separately, so the scale of elder-targeted fraud can only be inferred.
Dementia diagnosis in India remains low, so prevalence estimates and cost burdens are likely underestimated.

State estimates come from LASI-DAD Table 2; north-eastern states other than Assam were published only as a single group, so they share one value on the map, and several small states and union territories had no estimate and appear grey.
The cost figures from ADI are 2010 USD and reflect imputed unpaid care costs; actual out-of-pocket costs for Indian families will vary widely.
The GBD death estimates are modelled, not actual death-certificate counts, and are subject to coding changes and under-recording.
Fraud and abuse figures count only reported cases. Financial exploitation of a confused elder by relatives or acquaintances is rarely reported and is largely absent from any official record.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: Dementia already affects about one in thirteen Indians over 60, roughly 88 lakh people, and its true cost is hidden inside families as unpaid care and out-of-pocket spending, a burden set to nearly double as India ages to 1.69 crore by 2036.
requiredConcepts: LASI-DAD (Longitudinal Aging Study in India – Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia, 2018‑20): India’s first nationally representative, clinically adjudicated estimate — 7.4% of adults 60+ (95% CI 6.35‑8.51), age‑standardised 8.0%, roughly 8.8 million, projected to ~16.9 million by 2036
Dementia rises steeply with age: from 2.9% at 60–64 to 25.4% past 85, roughly doubling every five years after 70

Prevalence is higher in women (9.0% vs 5.8% men) and in rural India (8.4% vs 5.3% urban), and drops dramatically with schooling (10.3% no schooling → 1.5% middle school+) — these are associations, not clean causes
State prevalence ranges from ~4.5% in Delhi to ~11% in Jammu & Kashmir; several smaller states/UTs had no estimate
India’s crude prevalence looks lower than in rich countries mainly because of age structure, not biological protection; age‑standardised rates are broadly similar
Recorded deaths from dementia (IHME GBD, modelled) climbed from ~17,000 in 1980 to >1.4 lakh in 2023, but are a severe undercount; the jump after 2021 partly reflects a coding change

US study (Li et al., NBER 34659): household wealth begins to diverge about six years *before* dementia onset, ending roughly US $125,000 lower four years after; the gap is driven by impaired financial decision‑making, not overspending, and concentrates in stocks, bonds, mutual funds — no such gap appears for cancer, heart, lung, or arthritis

Timely diagnosis matters financially: in the US, the wealth gap flattens or reverses for those diagnosed in time, and widens for those with late/no diagnosis — highly relevant in India where most dementia goes undiagnosed

Only the US out‑of‑pocket medical excess (~US $1,668/year) may be tentatively PPP‑converted to roughly ₹35,000‑40,000 a year as a *caveated illustration*; the US wealth‑loss dollar amounts must never be converted

World Alzheimer Report 2010: societal cost per person in lower‑middle‑income (India’s band) was US $3,109/year vs US $32,865 in high‑income — the lower figure reflects mostly unpaid family care, not cheaper illness
In lower‑middle‑income, 65% of dementia cost is informal (unpaid) family care, compared to 40% in high‑income; unpaid does not mean free — it is paid in lost wages, overwhelmingly by women

India funds a large share of all health care out‑of‑pocket (OOPE as % of THE fell from 64.2% in 2014 to 43.4% in 2023), so even the medical slice of dementia care lands on families, on top of unpaid nursing

sectionPlan.heading: How quickly does dementia rise with age?
sectionPlan.job: Show why ageing drives the coming wave: prevalence jumps from 2.9% at 60–64 to a quarter past 85.
conceptsToExplain: prevalence within each age group
why dementia is overwhelmingly a condition of late old age
the near‑doubling every five years after 70
sectionPlan.caveat: These are modelled estimates from a single survey; all figures carry uncertainty.

sectionPlan.heading: How many people does that actually mean?
sectionPlan.job: Translate prevalence into headcount: 8.8 million in 2016, projected to 16.9 million by 2036 even if age‑specific risk stays flat.
conceptsToExplain: projection built on population ageing, not rising risk
why the absolute number matters for family and health system planning
sectionPlan.caveat: The 2036 projection assumes no change in age‑specific prevalence; real numbers could differ.

sectionPlan.heading: Who carries more: women, and rural India
sectionPlan.job: Show the uneven burden: women (~9%) vs men (~5.8%), rural (~8.4%) vs urban (~5.3%).
conceptsToExplain: prevalence by sex and residence
the women’s gap is partly because they live longer into high‑risk ages
rural‑urban differences may reflect education, nutrition, health access, and diagnostic patterns — not rural living itself
sectionPlan.caveat: These are crude prevalences, not adjusted for age or education; associations, not proven causes.

sectionPlan.heading: Does education make a difference?
sectionPlan.job: Reveal the steepest gradient: 10.3% with no schooling vs 1.5% with middle school or more.
conceptsToExplain: education as a measure of disadvantage and lifetime health
cognitive reserve as one possible mechanism
education also tracks income, nutrition, and health‑seeking behaviour
sectionPlan.caveat: Schooling is not a vaccine — it marks a web of advantages; the measured prevalence may also be lower because detection is harder in less‑educated groups.

sectionPlan.heading: Which states are hit hardest?
sectionPlan.job: Map the national patchwork: from ~4.5% in Delhi to ~11% in Jammu & Kashmir, with south and east generally higher.
conceptsToExplain: crude state‑level prevalence
the absence of estimates for several small states/UTs
the north‑east published only as a group
sectionPlan.caveat: State numbers are modelled from a sample; small‑state estimates are missing, and the north‑east is a single group.

sectionPlan.heading: Have deaths from dementia really risen eightfold?
sectionPlan.job: Present the mortality trend: from ~17,000 recorded deaths in 1980 to >1.4 lakh in 2023, with the caveats about under‑recording.
conceptsToExplain: dementia as a cause of death is badly under‑recorded
the long‑run rise reflects both ageing and better coding
the jump after 2021 partly reflects a coding change, so the focus is on the long climb
sectionPlan.caveat: GBD modelled estimates; real death counts on certificates are far lower. The post‑2021 spike is partly a statistical artifact.

sectionPlan.heading: What does America tell us about money slipping away before a diagnosis?
sectionPlan.job: Introduce the NBER evidence: wealth starts diverging ~6 years before dementia onset and ends about US $125,000 lower four years after.
conceptsToExplain: event‑time wealth gap
impaired financial decision‑making, not excess spending
why the study used placebo conditions (cancer, heart, etc.) to rule out other explanations
sectionPlan.caveat: This is US data; the mechanism may travel, but the dollar amounts do not, because older Indians hold very different assets.

sectionPlan.heading: Where exactly does the wealth leak from?
sectionPlan.job: Show that losses cluster in stocks, bonds, and mutual funds — assets that need active management — while earnings barely differ.
conceptsToExplain: portfolio composition of losses
why the gap signals judgement failure rather than medical bills or reduced work
the contrast with checking/savings and retirement accounts
sectionPlan.caveat: Again, US data. The specific asset classes (stocks, IRAs) are rare among elderly Indians, but the underlying idea — money at risk in assets that need periodic decisions — transfers to land, gold, informal loans, and small businesses.

sectionPlan.heading: What is the real cost of dementia care?
sectionPlan.job: Contrast societal costs across income groups: US $3,109/year in India’s band vs US $32,865 in rich countries — and explain why the headline gap is misleading.
conceptsToExplain: societal cost per person
the lower‑middle‑income figure is low because it omits the value of unpaid family care
only a small fraction is formal medical spending
sectionPlan.caveat: 2010 US dollars; real costs have risen since. The low figure for poor countries is not cheaper illness, it is invisible labour.

sectionPlan.heading: Why does the cost look so low in India?
sectionPlan.job: Show that 65% of dementia cost in lower‑middle‑income is unpaid family care, compared with 40% in high‑income — and why unpaid does not mean free.
conceptsToExplain: informal care share
unpaid care is paid in lost wages, lost years, and overwhelmingly by women
the absence of care‑home infrastructure in poorer countries
sectionPlan.caveat: The 65% is an approximate share; the real burden is larger if you price a daughter‑in‑law’s lost income or a woman’s forgone paid work.

sectionPlan.heading: Why does it land so heavily on families?
sectionPlan.job: Connect the dots: India’s out‑of‑pocket share of health spending is still 43.4%, so even the medical slice of dementia care hits household budgets directly.
conceptsToExplain: out‑of‑pocket expenditure (OOPE) as % of total health expenditure (THE)
the long decline from 64% to 43% still leaves a huge direct burden
dementia care therefore drains savings, gold, and land — and forces women out of paid work
sectionPlan.caveat: OOPE share is for all health care, not dementia specifically, but dementia’s long, chronic nature makes out‑of‑pocket spending especially punishing.

chartPlan.title: Dementia climbs steeply with age
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The first thing to know: dementia is a disease of late old age, with prevalence leaping from 2.9% to 25.4% across the age span.
chartPlan.howToRead: Each bar shows the percentage of people in that five‑year age band who have dementia. Follow the rise from left to right.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read this as the share of all dementia cases in each age group — it is the prevalence *within* each age band.

chartPlan.title: 88 lakh now, 1.69 crore by 2036
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Even if age‑specific risk stays flat, India’s ageing population will nearly double the raw headcount of dementia.
chartPlan.howToRead: The two bars (or points) show estimated cases in 2016 and projected to 2036. Focus on the near doubling.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: This is not a forecast of rising risk per person; it is a projection of numbers driven by demographic ageing alone.

chartPlan.title: Who carries more: women, and rural India
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The burden is uneven: women and rural Indians bear a noticeably higher share.
chartPlan.howToRead: Compare the bars for women vs men, and rural vs urban. Small differences in percentage points mask large numbers of people.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Do not infer that being female or rural *causes* dementia — these are crude associations tangled with age, education, and health history.

chartPlan.title: Dementia falls sharply with schooling
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The steepest gradient of all is education, hinting at how much systemic disadvantage shapes brain health.
chartPlan.howToRead: The bars represent three broad education levels. Note the drop from 10.3% to 1.5%.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Education is not a direct shield; it captures a cluster of advantages, and detection may vary across groups. Do not read the 1.5% as a ‘safe’ level for all time.

chartPlan.title: Where dementia is most common
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The map shows a national spread from about 4.5% in Delhi to roughly 11% in Jammu & Kashmir.
chartPlan.howToRead: Darker‑shaded states have higher estimated prevalence among adults 60+. Hover or tap for the figure.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Missing states and UTs (white) lack estimates; the north‑east is shown as one group. State boundaries do not create neat health differences.

chartPlan.title: Deaths recorded from dementia have risen eightfold
chartPlan.whyShowThis: As Indians live longer, dementia emerges in the mortality data, climbing from ~17,000 to >1.4 lakh modelled deaths.
chartPlan.howToRead: A single line over time. The steep post‑2021 jump is partly a coding change; focus on the long‑term rise.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: These are modelled estimates, not actual death‑certificate counts. The true number is likely much higher because dementia is under‑diagnosed at death.

chartPlan.title: America: money trouble starts before the diagnosis
chartPlan.whyShowThis: US evidence shows household wealth begins to erode ~6 years *before* dementia is diagnosed, ending about US $125,000 lower — evidence for a financial‑judgement mechanism.
chartPlan.howToRead: Each bar shows the wealth gap (in thousands of US dollars) compared with similar dementia‑free households at that event time. Negative values mean less wealth.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: This is US data. The dollar amounts do not apply to India. Only the *pattern* — money problems surface early and are driven by impaired decisions — is what matters here.

chartPlan.title: America: the gap sits in hard-to-manage assets
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The losses are concentrated in stocks, bonds, and mutual funds — assets demanding active management — while cash accounts and retirement accounts differ little.
chartPlan.howToRead: For each asset type, compare the dark bar (developing dementia) with the light bar (matched control). The gap is largest in market‑linked securities.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Again, US asset classes are not Indian. The takeaway is that assets that need periodic decisions are at risk, not that elderly Indians hold US stocks.

chartPlan.title: What a year of dementia care costs
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The 2010 global cost figure for India’s income band, US $3,109, is a fraction of the US $32,865 in rich countries — but it is mostly *time*, not invoices.
chartPlan.howToRead: Four bars, one per World Bank income group. The cost escalates with income, but the composition changes even more.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Do not conclude that dementia is cheap in India. The low figure leaves out the lion’s share — unpaid family care — which the next chart reveals.

chartPlan.title: The poorer the country, the more care is unpaid
chartPlan.whyShowThis: In lower‑middle‑income countries, 65% of total dementia cost is informal (family) care, versus 40% in high‑income — unpaid does not mean free.
chartPlan.howToRead: Three bars showing the % of total societal cost that is unpaid family labour. Compare the 65% bar for India’s band with the 40% bar.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: ‘Unpaid’ means it never appears in any budget, but it is paid in lost wages and lost years, mostly by women.

chartPlan.title: Why it lands on families: India pays out of pocket
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Even the formal medical costs of dementia largely come out of household pockets. India’s out‑of‑pocket share of all health spending has fallen but remains high at 43.4%.
chartPlan.howToRead: A line chart from 2014 to 2023. The downward trend is progress, but the level is still high relative to countries with stronger health insurance.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: This is the share of *all* health spending that households pay directly. Dementia is not broken out, but the chronic nature of the disease makes each percentage point hurt more.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Longitudinal Aging Study in India – Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia. A nationally representative survey that sent trained clinicians to assess cognitive function in a sample of older Indians, instead of using hospital records.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It provides India’s first robust, home‑grown estimate of how common dementia really is — the backbone of every figure on this page.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The share of people in a group who have a condition at a given time. Think ‘how many in every hundred have it right now’, not ‘how many will ever get it’.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: All the percentages shown (2.9%, 9%, etc.) are prevalence — the burden sitting in the community today.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A range around an estimate that reflects statistical uncertainty. If the study were repeated 100 times, the true value would fall inside this range 95 times. It does not mean there is a 95% chance the true value is inside — that is a common misinterpretation.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: LASI-DAD’s estimate of 7.4% (95% CI 6.35–8.51) reminds us that the number is not exact; the real prevalence is likely somewhere in that band.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A summary rate that imagines each country had the same age distribution (a standard population). It strips out the effect of a country’s age mix so we can compare disease risk fairly.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India’s crude prevalence looks low because India is young. Age‑standardised rates show the risk is not so different from richer, older countries.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A huge, continuously updated study by IHME that models health loss from hundreds of diseases for every country, combining surveys, hospital data, and death records to fill gaps.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: GBD provides the only long‑run trend of dementia deaths for India; without it, we would have almost no mortality numbers.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A conversion rate that compares what money actually buys in different countries, instead of using market exchange rates. US$1 converted at PPP buys a basket of goods in India similar to what US$1 buys in the US.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It is the least misleading way to turn a US medical‑cost number into a rough rupee illustration, but it remains an illustration, not an actual Indian price.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The share of all health spending in a country that is paid directly by households at the point of care — not through insurance, government schemes, or employers.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: High OOPE means even diagnosed dementia care drains family budgets immediately, on top of the unpaid nursing.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The sum of all money spent on health in a country in a year, from government budgets, insurance, employers, and households.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: When we say OOPE is 43.4%, that is 43.4% of this total. The denominator is all health spending, not just the private market.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Unpaid care provided by family members — bathing, feeding, watching, managing money — that replaces what would be paid professional or institutional care in a richer system.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: In India, roughly two‑thirds of the total cost of dementia is this invisible labour, and it shows up nowhere in budgets or insurance claims.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The brain’s ability to improvise and find alternate ways of getting a job done, built up over a lifetime of education, complex work, and social engagement. It does not prevent the underlying disease, but it can delay the point at which symptoms appear.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The steep education gradient in dementia prevalence is partly explained by cognitive reserve — more‑schooled brains may cope longer before clinical detection — but education also brings better nutrition and health care, so the effect is mixed.

proseRules: No AI tells (delve, tapestry, interplay, crucial, moreover, furthermore, in conclusion).
No outside facts; every number and source must come from this evidence packet or the supplied locked numbers.
No calculations unless the evidence packet supplies the derived number explicitly.
Every H2 is a reader question that the section genuinely answers, tied to one planned chart in order.
Never convert the US wealth‑gap dollar figures into rupees — the mechanism travels, the amounts do not.
If a single rupee illustration is given (oope‑medical excess), it must be PPP‑converted, caveated as US‑sourced, presented as a range (₹35,000–40,000), and never called an actual Indian cost.
Keep the three layers distinct: Indian scale (LASI‑DAD), US mechanism (NBER), and hidden Indian cost structure (ADI + NHA).
Present estimates as estimates; use ranges and caveats, never false precision.
Do not call any association a cause unless the evidence proves it.
Do not compare India to any peer unless that comparison is in the locked numbers or source summaries.

plannedCharts.title: Dementia climbs steeply with age
plannedCharts.subtitle: LASI-DAD 2018-20 (Lee et al., Alzheimer's & Dementia 2023) · estimated prevalence by age band
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The first thing to know: dementia is overwhelmingly a disease of late old age. It jumps from about 3% in the early 60s to a quarter of everyone past 85.

plannedCharts.title: 88 lakh now, 1.69 crore by 2036
plannedCharts.subtitle: LASI-DAD · estimated cases, 2016 population base and 2036 projection
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Because India is ageing fast, the headcount is set to nearly double in twenty years even if the risk at each age stays flat.

plannedCharts.title: Who carries more: women, and rural India
plannedCharts.subtitle: LASI-DAD 2018-20 · crude prevalence among adults 60+
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Dementia is not spread evenly. Women carry noticeably more of it than men, and rural Indians more than city dwellers.

plannedCharts.title: Dementia falls sharply with schooling
plannedCharts.subtitle: LASI-DAD 2018-20 · crude prevalence by education
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The steepest gradient of all is education: those with no schooling have many times the measured prevalence of those who finished middle school.

plannedCharts.title: Where dementia is most common
plannedCharts.subtitle: LASI-DAD 2018-20 · estimated prevalence among adults 60+, by state
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The map runs from about 4.5% in Delhi to roughly 11% in Jammu & Kashmir, with the south and east generally higher than the north-western plains.

plannedCharts.title: Deaths recorded from dementia have risen eightfold
plannedCharts.subtitle: IHME Global Burden of Disease 2023 · estimated annual deaths from Alzheimer's & other dementias, India
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: As Indians live longer and other killers recede, dementia surfaces in the mortality data: recorded deaths have climbed from about 17,000 in 1980 to over 1.4 lakh.

plannedCharts.title: America: money trouble starts before the diagnosis
plannedCharts.unit: US$1,000s of net worth vs similar households
plannedCharts.subtitle: NBER WP 34659 (Li et al. 2026) · US Health & Retirement Study · evidence from the United States
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This is US data, shown to explain the mechanism, not to put a rupee figure on India. American households heading into dementia fall behind similar households starting about six years before onset, ending roughly $125,000 poorer.

plannedCharts.title: America: the gap sits in hard-to-manage assets
plannedCharts.unit: US$1,000s held, two years before onset
plannedCharts.subtitle: NBER WP 34659 · means two years before onset · evidence from the United States
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The losses concentrate in stocks, bonds and investment accounts, the assets that need active judgement to manage. Earnings barely differ, and cancer or heart disease show no such gap, which points at decision-making, not spending.

plannedCharts.title: What a year of dementia care costs
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Alzheimer Report 2010 (ADI / Wimo & Prince) · societal cost per person, by country income group
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: On paper, dementia looks far cheaper in poorer countries. India sat in the lower-middle band at about US$3,100 a year per person, against nearly US$33,000 in rich countries.

plannedCharts.title: The poorer the country, the more care is unpaid
plannedCharts.unit: % of dementia cost that is unpaid family care
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Alzheimer Report 2010 (ADI) · share of total cost that is informal (family) care
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Here is why India's cost looks low and is in fact hidden: in its income band about two-thirds of the entire cost of dementia is unpaid family labour that never enters any budget.

plannedCharts.title: Why it lands on families: India pays out of pocket
plannedCharts.subtitle: National Health Accounts (MoHFW) · out-of-pocket spending as a share of total health expenditure, India
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Even the medical slice of dementia care falls on households, because India funds a large share of all health care straight out of family pockets.
